entries.title: Putin pledges Russia’s support to end US-led war on Iran
entries.summary: The Russian and Iranian presidents met in Turkmenistan ahead of regional summit.
entries.content:
The Russian and Iranian presidents met in Turkmenistan ahead of regional summit.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has told Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian that Russia will “do everything” to help end the United States-led war on Iran, Russian news agencies reported.

The two leaders met in Turkmenistan on Thursday ahead of the summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States, a group of former Soviet nations.

“You know our position. On our part, we are ready to do everything we can to help you resolve this situation,” Interfax news agency said Putin told Pezeshkian.

“We know that Iran is making real efforts to end the conflict, which broke out through no fault of its own, no fault of Iran’s,” Putin said, according to Russian media.

Putin also noted what he called a “positive evolution” in Iran-Russia relations.

In a call on Wednesday, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow is prepared to mediate efforts to end the war in the Middle East, Iran’s IRNA news agency reported.

Putin and Pezeshkian also met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan last month.

Strategic partnership

The two countries, which are under heavy Western sanctions, have reinforced diplomatic and military ties.

Last year, Moscow and Tehran signed a “comprehensive strategic partnership treaty” that covers areas from trade and military cooperation to science, culture and education.

Ukraine and Western countries have accused Iran of supplying Russia with Shahed drones and short-range missiles for use in the Ukraine war. Russia has also been accused of supplying data to Iran for its attacks on US targets in the Middle East.

The meeting came as Iran-US talks stand at an apparent impasse.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before the November 3 US midterm congressional elections, saying the two countries are ‌‌holding “productive” talks about ending the ongoing war.

Diplomatic efforts to resolve Russia’s offensive in Ukraine also appear deadlocked, even as both sides intensify attacks.

entries.title: French giants Bordeaux relegated to sixth tier for financial irregularities
entries.summary: Six-time French champions Bordeaux, the club where Zinedine Zidane made his name, to play in sixth tier after sanctions.
entries.content:
Six-time French champions Bordeaux, the club where Zinedine Zidane made his name, to play in sixth tier after sanctions.

Six-time French champions Bordeaux, sanctioned in the summer for financial irregularities, will play in the sixth tier of French football this season, the Nouvelle-Aquitaine league confirmed on Thursday.

Bordeaux were sanctioned for failing to provide the roughly 10 million euros ($11.6m) needed for the 2025-26 and 2026-27 financial years and to meet debt payments.

Once one of France’s leading football clubs and the team where the country’s new head coach, Zinedine Zidane, made his name, Bordeaux was sold last month for a symbolic one euro to US-based investment group Park Bench, which agreed to take on the remaining debt.

Two days after appearing before the Nouvelle-Aquitaine league oversight commission, which approved its recovery budget and issued “a positive opinion on their possible participation in Regional 1”, the club was unanimously approved to play in the top regional tier.

“Rebuilding can now begin,” said Dominique Delport, the new president chosen by Park Bench, speaking to the AFP news agency.

The new owners are due in commercial court on October 20 to ratify the new continuation plan, which now runs over 12 years, with the debt halved from 26 million to 13 million euros.

The team is largely amateur, though the club can field five players on professional contracts, one of whom will be former Ligue 1 striker Baptiste Guillaume.

The club has produced many big names of French football, including academy products Bixente Lizarazu and Christophe Dugarry, who both played alongside Zidane in the 1998 World Cup-winning team.

More than a decade earlier, Alain Giresse and Jean Tigana were part of a celebrated France midfield that won the 1984 European Championship.

However, they were relegated to Ligue 2 in 2022 and then placed under judicial restructuring in 2024, which caused them to relinquish their professional status and their highly rated academy.

entries.title: What Man City charges anger Liverpool before Premier League game?
entries.summary: Clubs reportedly want reimbursements after Man City charges - one of those, Liverpool, are first opponent in fallout.
entries.content:
Clubs are reportedly exploring claims after Man City verdict – one of those, Liverpool, are first opponent in fallout.

Manchester City are preparing for their first football match since receiving a guilty verdict for multiple breaches of Premier League financial rules and – of course – their opponent on Sunday is one of the clubs that hold grievances over their losses during the seasons in question.

Liverpool’s Anfield crowd is expected to deliver an angry reception for the Premier League clash, and City manager Enzo Maresca and his players must prepare for the backlash to continue throughout the game itself.

City have protested their innocence and have appealed the verdict that went against them on more than 100 charges of financial wrongdoing.

Still, the scandal remains the biggest in the history of club football’s richest, most competitive and most popular league, and the backlash from the stands is likely to linger long after any appeal outcome or potential punishments are finalised.

The current crop of players and staff are quite simply going to have to face the music for charges that stretch from 2009 to 2018.

The fact that their opening match after the international window, when the guilty verdict was delivered, is at Anfield is something that a scriptwriter may even pause to think is outlandish.

“If they want an understanding of how angry the game ⁠is going to be, then Anfield will tell them like you would never believe,” former Manchester United captain and England defender Gary Neville declared recently on The Overlap podcast.

“I suspect there may be banners, there will certainly be chanting. There will be a reception like you have never seen for them at Anfield… it will be a brutal day.”

Why are Liverpool set to give Man City an angry reception?

Of all the clubs that finished second best to City since the Abu Dhabi buyout, Liverpool will argue that they have been among the hardest hit.

There is a growing feeling that any titles that City are stripped of should be awarded to their nearest rivals, or defeated finalists, during the period investigated.

For Liverpool, however, their two closest calls with City came after 2018.

Under former coach Jurgen Klopp, Liverpool won the Premier League in 2020, but the team also finished second to Pep Guardiola’s City by one point in the 2018-19 and 2021-22 seasons.

Both were memorable title races that raised the bar in terms of points earned and the standard of football played.

Neither will see Liverpool retrospectively awarded the title if the Premier League does indeed choose to go down that path regarding honours won in the seasons that were under investigation.

Liverpool’s fans will assert, and most likely vociferously argue on Sunday, that what helped City reach that level was nearly a decade of rule-breaking, as the independent panel has found.

Liverpool do, however, have a claim to at least one title in the period in question.

The Reds, under Brendan Rodgers, finished runners-up by two points to City in 2013-2014 – Steven Gerrard’s infamous slip in a match against Chelsea the moment etched on everyone’s memory from that campaign.

It left the Anfield faithful continuing their wait for a first top-flight title since 1990.

Only weeks earlier, Gerrard was the star of the show as Liverpool beat City 3-2 to seemingly put one hand on the elusive title.

Any retrospective award of titles could see club legend Gerrard finally hold a Premier League winner’s medal.

Do any of Man City’s current setup remain from the period of the charges?

Aside from Phil Foden, who is suspended for the match, no current member of City’s squad even played for the club from 2009-2018.

Enzo Maresca, who was a youth-team coach for City in 2020-21 and was assistant to Guardiola in 2022-2023, took over as City’s first-team manager only in June.

Still, they will be the ones bearing the brunt of the widespread discontent from fan bases up and down the country in the coming months.

What will be intriguing is who from City’s ownership or board attends the Liverpool game.

How much will the matter weigh on the players under the most intense pressure? And what will be the reaction of City’s match-going supporters, with the future of their club so uncertain – the potential sanctions include a huge points deduction, even expulsion from the Premier League – and the violations of its ownership clear for all to see in the commission’s verdict?

City lead the league with five wins from five games – all of which were played when the club was being accused of those financial breaches.

Now the guilty verdict has arrived, it’s time to see the impact on the team – and the reaction of its rivals.

entries.title: Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives
entries.summary: The National Medal of Science is annually given to scientists and engineers for major contributions in their fields.
entries.content:
The National Medal of Science is given annually to scientists and engineers for major contributions in their fields.

United States President Donald Trump has awarded the country’s most prestigious honours in science and engineering to executives from top technology firms including SpaceX, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia.

On Thursday, Trump presented the National Medal of Science to billionaire SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Lisa Su of the semiconductor firm AMD.

Two more recipients received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation: Michael Dell of Dell Technologies and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

At the award ceremony, Trump credited the honourees with “helping pioneer an incredible future for America”.

“Because of these people here, we will always be on top. No one else can compete with us,” Trump said.

Five of the six people receiving medals on Thursday were born outside the US. Four are among the 10 wealthiest people in the world, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The award ceremony took place hours after the Trump administration announced it was suspending Microsoft and other top tech companies from using the H-1B visa system, which allows companies to hire skilled foreign workers and put them on a path towards permanent residency in the US.

The suspension, officials said, was due to the companies allegedly using the system in a fraudulent manner.

White House builds ties with Silicon Valley

The medal ceremony was the latest example of what critics see as an increasingly close relationship between Silicon Valley tech executives and the second Trump administration.

Powerful companies like Amazon, Meta and Nvidia contributed money to Trump’s second inauguration, and several high-profile industry leaders attended his swearing-in, including Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

Trump, for his part, has pledged to slash regulations and position the US “as the world leader in artificial intelligence”.

He has also touted self-regulation in the AI industry amid concerns about the safety of the technology.

Several of the tech entrepreneurs honoured on Thursday have forged close ties to the White House, through political and business dealings.

The South Africa-born Musk, for example, was the largest contributor to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and has been a supporter of right-wing causes around the world, which he amplifies on his social media platform, X.

He briefly served as a special adviser to the president during the first months of Trump’s second term, helping to lead the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and its efforts to downsize the federal government.

Around the time he left DOGE, however, Musk and Trump had a public falling-out over the president’s tax-and-spending plans.

The two have since reconciled. On Thursday, Trump hailed Musk as “our modern-day Thomas Edison” and an “industrial titan”, citing his work with the aerospace company SpaceX and the carmaker Tesla.

“Few Americans in history have done more to advance America’s national interest than Elon in one field after another,” Trump said.

Another honouree, Dell, has been a financial backer of the president’s efforts to launch Trump Accounts, a scheme to enrol American children born during Trump’s second term into government-backed investment accounts.

Dell and his wife Susan Dell committed $6.25bn to the programme last year.

Separately, the White House entered into a deal in August for the US government to take a 15 percent cut of any AI chip sales that Nvidia and AMD make with China.

Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder, later invested in the struggling US tech firm Intel. He is reported to be among the donors financing Trump’s plans for a new White House ballroom.

The National Medal of Science was first awarded in 1963 to Theodore von Karman, a pioneer in aerospace engineering who fled anti-Semitism in Europe during World War II.

He went on to help found the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology.

Nominations for the award are solicited by the National Science Foundation, and the recipients are ultimately selected by a committee appointed by the president.

entries.title: South Africa protests turn violent amid rage over asylum ruling
entries.summary: Several cars torched and foreign-run businesses forced to shut in Johannesburg's Soweto and coastal city of Durban.
entries.content:
Several cars torched and foreign-run businesses forced to shut in Johannesburg’s Soweto and coastal city of Durban.

Anti-migrant protests in two cities in South Africa have turned ⁠violent, with the government blaming disinformation about a court ruling on asylum seekers.

Violence erupted on Thursday in Johannesburg’s Soweto township and the east coast port city of Durban, with two dozens cars set ablaze and foreign-run businesses forced to close, police said.

The unrest followed demonstrations demanding that refugee centres stop processing asylum applications.

Acting National Police Commissioner Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane on Thursday said 10 vehicles were torched in Johannesburg and 14 in Durban, where three people were arrested.

In Soweto, a Reuters reporter saw residents carrying groceries out of a shop they said was owned by a person from Somalia, whom they chased away. Those residents fled after police arrived.

In Durban, a Reuters reporter saw cars torched in the urban centre, where foreign-owned shops were also looted. AFP reporters in the city said police opened fire with rubber bullets to disperse protesters who reportedly set alight a business run by foreigners.

The protesters are opposed to a July Constitutional Court decision that removes procedural barriers to seeking asylum, including for people who entered South Africa irregularly, lacked asylum transit visas, or missed reporting deadlines.

On Thursday, the government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration held an urgent briefing to address overcrowding at asylum offices after implementing the ruling. A day prior, the committee said all its offices were overwhelmed by the number of incoming applications.

Government spokesperson William Baloyi said ‌the violence was triggered by people spreading deliberately false information about the constitutional court ruling.

Baloyi said the court decision had been widely misrepresented, and that it did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or other legal rights to undocumented migrants.

“We are ⁠deeply concerned by what is going on now,” he added.

Months of protests by populist, anti-immigrant groups against undocumented foreign nationals, demanding they leave South Africa, have led tens of thousands to flee, some repatriated by their governments.

Three decades since apartheid ended, South Africa remains deeply unequal and about a third of people are out of work. Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fuelling crime and straining public services, although such claims are not supported by evidence.
